{{Short description|Concept in number theory}}In [[number theory]], '''natural density''', also referred to as '''asymptotic density''' or '''arithmetic density''', is a measure of how "large" a [[subset]] of the [[Set (mathematics)|set]] of [[natural number]]s is. It relies chiefly on the [[probability]] of encountering members of the desired subset when combing through the [[Interval (mathematics)|interval]] {{math|[1, {{var|n}}]}} as {{mvar|n}} grows large.

For example, it may seem intuitively that there are more [[positive integer]]s than [[square number|perfect square]]s, because every perfect square is already positive and yet many other positive integers exist besides. However, the set of positive integers is not in fact larger than the set of perfect squares: both sets are [[Infinite set|infinite]] and [[countable]] and can therefore be put in [[bijection|one-to-one correspondence]]. Nevertheless if one goes through the natural numbers, the squares become increasingly scarce. The notion of natural density makes this intuition precise for many, but not all, subsets of the naturals (see [[Schnirelmann density]], which is similar to natural density but defined for all subsets of <math>\mathbb{N}</math>).

If an integer is randomly selected from the interval {{math|[1, {{var|n}}]}}, then the probability that it belongs to {{mvar|A}} is the ratio of the number of elements of {{mvar|A}} in {{math|[1, {{var|n}}]}} to the total number of elements in {{math|[1, {{var|n}}]}}. If this probability tends to some [[Limit (mathematics)|limit]] as {{mvar|n}} tends to infinity, then this limit is referred to as the asymptotic density of {{mvar|A}}. This notion can be understood as a kind of probability of choosing a number from the set {{mvar|A}}. Indeed, the asymptotic density (as well as some other types of densities) is studied in [[probabilistic number theory]].

== Definition ==
A subset {{mvar|A}} of positive integers has natural density {{mvar|α}} if the proportion of elements of {{mvar|A}} among all  [[natural number]]s from {{math|1}} to {{mvar|n}} converges to {{mvar|α}} as {{mvar|n}} tends to infinity.

More explicitly, if one defines for any natural number {{mvar|n}} the counting [[Function (mathematics)|function]] {{math|{{var|a}}({{var|n}})}} as the number of elements of {{mvar|A}} less than or equal to {{mvar|n}}, then the natural density of {{mvar|A}} being {{mvar|α}} exactly means that<ref name=Ten261/>

{{bi|left=1.6|{{math|{{var|a}}({{var|n}})/{{var|n}} → {{var|α}}}} as {{math|{{var|n}} → ∞}}.}}

It follows from the definition that if a set {{mvar|A}} has natural density {{mvar|α}} then {{math|0 ≤ {{var|α}} ≤ 1}}.

=== Upper and lower asymptotic density ===

Let <math>A</math> be a subset of the set of natural numbers <math>\mathbb{N}=\{1,2,\ldots\}.</math> For any <math>n \in \mathbb{N}</math>, define <math>A(n)</math> to be the intersection <math>A(n)=\{1,2,\ldots,n\} \cap A,</math> and let <math>a(n)=|A(n)|</math> be the number of elements of <math>A</math> less than or equal to <math>n</math>.

Define the ''upper asymptotic density'' <math>\overline{d}(A)</math> of <math>A</math> (also called the "upper density") by
<math display="block"> \overline{d}(A) = \limsup_{n \rightarrow \infty} \frac{a(n)}{n} </math>
where lim sup is the [[limit superior]].

Similarly, define the ''lower asymptotic density'' <math>\underline{d}(A)</math> of <math>A</math> (also called the "lower density") by
<math display="block"> \underline{d}(A) = \liminf_{n \rightarrow \infty} \frac{ a(n) }{n} </math>
where lim inf is the [[limit inferior]]. One may say <math>A</math> has asymptotic density <math>d(A)</math> if <math>\underline{d}(A)=\overline{d}(A)</math>, in which case <math>d(A)</math> is equal to this common value.

This definition can be restated in the following way:
<math display="block"> d(A)=\lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} \frac{a(n)}{n} </math>
if this limit exists.<ref>Nathanson (2000) pp.256–257</ref>

These definitions may equivalently{{Citation needed|date=May 2024}} be expressed in the following way. Given a subset <math>A</math> of <math>\mathbb{N}</math>, write it as an increasing sequence indexed by the natural numbers:
<math display="block">A = \{a_1 < a_2 < \ldots\}.</math>
Then
<math display="block">\underline{d}(A) = \liminf_{n \rightarrow \infty} \frac{n}{a_n},</math>
<math display="block">\overline{d}(A) = \limsup_{n \rightarrow \infty} \frac{n}{a_n}</math>
and
<math display="block">d(A) = \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} \frac{n}{a_n}</math>
if the limit exists.

A somewhat weaker notion of density is the ''upper Banach density'' <math>d^*(A)</math> of a set <math>A \subseteq \mathbb{N}.</math>  This is defined as{{Citation needed|date=January 2025}}
<math display="block"> d^*(A) = \limsup_{N-M \rightarrow \infty} \frac{| A \cap \{M, M+1, \ldots , N\}|}{N-M+1}. </math>

== Properties and examples ==
{{More citations needed|section|date=January 2025}}
* For any [[finite set]] ''F'' of positive integers, ''d''(''F'') = 0.
* If ''d''(''A'') exists for some set ''A'' and ''A''<sup>c</sup> denotes its [[Complement (set theory)|complement set]] with respect to <math>\N</math>, then ''d''(''A''<sup>c</sup>) = 1 − ''d''(''A'').
** Corollary: If <math>F\subset \N </math> is finite (including the case <math>F=\emptyset</math>),  <math>d(\N \setminus F)=1.</math>
* If <math>d(A), d(B),</math> and <math>d(A \cup B)</math> exist, then <math display="block">
\max\{d(A),d(B)\} \leq d(A\cup B) \leq \min\{d(A)+d(B),1\}.</math>
* If <math>A = \{n^2 : n \in \N\}</math> is the set of all squares, then ''d''(''A'') = 0.
* If <math>A = \{2n : n \in \N\}</math> is the set of all even numbers, then ''d''(''A'') = 0.5. Similarly, for any arithmetical progression <math>A = \{an + b : n \in \N\}</math> we get <math>d(A) = \tfrac{1}{a}.</math>
* For the set ''P'' of all [[prime number|prime]]s we get from the [[prime number theorem]] that ''d''(''P'') = 0.
* The set of all [[square-free integer]]s has density <math>\tfrac{6}{\pi^2}.</math> More generally, the set of all ''n''th-power-free numbers for any natural ''n'' has density <math>\tfrac{1}{\zeta(n)},</math> where <math>\zeta(n)</math> is the [[Riemann zeta function]].
* The set of [[abundant number]]s has non-zero density.<ref name="HT95">{{cite book | zbl=0653.10001 | last1=Hall | first1=Richard R. | last2=Tenenbaum | first2=Gérald | author2-link=Gérald Tenenbaum | title=Divisors | series=Cambridge Tracts in Mathematics | volume=90 | location=Cambridge | publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]] | year=1988 | isbn=978-0-521-34056-4 | page=95 }}</ref>  Marc Deléglise showed in 1998 that the density of the set of abundant numbers is between 0.2474 and 0.2480.<ref name="Del1998">{{cite journal | first=Marc | last=Deléglise | title=Bounds for the density of abundant integers | journal=Experimental Mathematics | volume=7 | issue=2 | year=1998 | pages=137–143 | url=http://projecteuclid.org/euclid.em/1048515661 | mr=1677091 | zbl=0923.11127 | issn=1058-6458 | doi=10.1080/10586458.1998.10504363}}</ref>
* The set <math display="block">A = \bigcup_{n=0}^\infty \left \{2^{2n},\ldots,2^{2n+1}-1 \right \}</math> of numbers whose binary expansion contains an odd number of digits is an example of a set which does not have an asymptotic density, since the upper density of this set is <math display="block">\overline d(A)=\lim_{m \to \infty}\frac{1+2^2+\cdots +2^{2m}}{2^{2m+1}-1}=\lim_{m \to\infty} \frac{2^{2m+2}-1}{3(2^{2m+1}-1)} = \frac 23,</math> whereas its lower density is <math display="block">\underline d(A)=\lim_{m \to\infty}\frac{1+2^2+\cdots +2^{2m}}{2^{2m+2}-1}=\lim_{m \to\infty} \frac{2^{2m+2}-1}{3(2^{2m+2}-1)} = \frac 13.</math>
* The set of numbers whose [[decimal expansion]] begins with the digit 1 similarly has no natural density: the lower density is 1/9 and the upper density is 5/9.<ref name="Ten261">Tenenbaum (1995) p.261</ref> (See [[Benford's law]].)
* Consider an [[equidistributed sequence]] <math>\{\alpha_n\}_{n\in\N}</math> in <math>[0,1]</math> and define a monotone family <math>\{A_x\}_{x\in[0,1]}</math> of sets: <math display="block">A_x:=\{n\in\N : \alpha_n<x \}.</math> Then, by definition, <math>d(A_x)= x</math> for all <math>x</math>.
* If ''S'' is a set of positive upper density then [[Szemerédi's theorem]] states that ''S'' contains arbitrarily large finite [[arithmetic progression]]s, and the [[Furstenberg–Sárközy theorem]] states that some two members of ''S'' differ by a square number.

==Other density functions==
Other density functions on subsets of the natural numbers may be defined analogously. For example, the ''logarithmic density'' of a set ''A'' is defined as the limit (if it exists)
<math display="block">
 \mathbf{\delta}(A) = \lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{1}{\log x} \sum_{n \in A, n \le x} \frac{1}{n}.
</math>

Upper and lower logarithmic densities are defined analogously.

The intuition behind using <math> \tfrac{1}{n} </math> in the summand comes from the fact that the [[Harmonic series (mathematics)|harmonic series]] asymptotically approaches <math> \log n + \gamma </math>, where <math> \gamma = 0.577\ldots </math> is the [[Euler–Mascheroni constant]]. Thus, this definition ensures that the logarithmic density of the natural numbers is <math> 1 </math>.

For the set of multiples of an integer sequence, the [[Davenport–Erdős theorem]] states that the natural density, when it exists, is equal to the logarithmic density.<ref>{{citation
 | last = Hall | first = Richard R.
 | doi = 10.1017/CBO9780511566011
 | isbn = 978-0-521-40424-2
 | mr = 1414678
 | at = Theorem 0.2, p. 5
 | publisher = Cambridge University Press, Cambridge
 | series = Cambridge Tracts in Mathematics
 | title = Sets of multiples
 | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=40g9YJIck0QC&pg=PA5
 | volume = 118
 | year = 1996}}</ref>
